groups.content:
Pangolins

Appearance

  • the only mammals with scales, which are made of [1]
  • the underside has no scales but is protected by fine [2]

Movement

  • several species walk on their back legs and use their [3] to stay balanced

Feeding

  • catch ants and termites with a long, sticky [4]
  • swallow [5] which help to break down food in the stomach

Senses

  • have poor eyesight and depend mainly on [6] to find prey

Reading Passage 2 has six paragraphs, A-F.

Which paragraph contains the following information?

Write the correct letter, A-F, in boxes 14-16 on your answer sheet.

NB You may use any letter more than once.

Questions 17-22

Complete the summary below.

Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for each answer.
groups.content:
Why do we ruminate?

Some people believe that rumination helps them deal with problems, while others see it as an indication of a [17] personality. In fact, people who ruminate come up with fewer [18] to their problems. Brain scans have shown unusual activity in a network connected with areas that process [19].

Rumination is common among people who feel they must meet others' [20], and it is often triggered by situations which are still [21]. One reason it continues is that it seems [22], although in reality it only strengthens negative feelings.

groups.instruction:
Questions 27-32

Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in Reading Passage 3?

In boxes 27-32 on your answer sheet, write

YES if the statement agrees with the claims of the writer
NO if the statement contradicts the claims of the writer
NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this

Questions 33-37

Complete the summary using the list of phrases, A-H, below.

Write the correct letter, A-H, in boxes 33-37 on your answer sheet.

A   fixed rules
B   frequent complaints
C   national teams
D   personal judgement
E   broad agreement
F   digital model
G   second opinion
H   individual faults
groups.content:
Scoring with sensors

While the gymnast performed, Kovacs was able to watch a [33] on a screen beside her. However, the system's role was only to give judges a [34]. A gymnast's execution score depends on the number of [35] that the judges notice, and deciding how serious these are has always required [36]. This explains why major championships have often been followed by [37].

questions.explanation: Answer: keratin Paragraph 2: 'A pangolin's scales are made of keratin , the same material as human fingernails'.
Answer: hair Paragraph 2: the underside 'has no scales but is covered in fine hair '.
Answer: tail Paragraph 3: several species walk mainly on their back legs, 'using the tail for balance'. The front claws are tucked underneath, so they are not used for balance.
Answer: tongue Paragraph 4: 'they catch insects with an extraordinarily long, sticky tongue '.
Answer: stones Paragraph 4: 'pangolins swallow small stones , which collect in the stomach and help to grind up their food'. 'Break down' paraphrases 'grind up'.
Answer: smell Paragraph 5: 'Their eyesight is poor, and they locate their prey mainly by smell .'
Answer: TRUE Paragraph 7: 'The four Asian species are found across a wide area , from Pakistan and India in the west to southern China, Indonesia and the Philippines in the east.'
Answer: FALSE Paragraph 7: the Indian pangolin 'occurs in grasslands and forests and even on farmland '. This contradicts the claim that it avoids agricultural land.

Answer: NOT GIVEN Paragraph 8 says where Temminck's ground pangolin lives ('the drier savannas of eastern and southern parts of the continent'), but does not compare the size of its range with the other African species.
Answer: TRUE Paragraph 9: the scales 'are used in traditional medicines even though they have no proven medical value '.

Answer: NOT GIVEN Paragraph 9 says that 'large shipments of scales from Africa have been seized in Asian ports', but it gives no figures and says nothing about whether the quantity has risen every year.
Answer: NOT GIVEN Paragraph 10 states that trade 'was banned' in 2016, but gives no information about whether the ban has reduced the number of pangolins being caught.
Answer: TRUE Paragraph 10: pangolins 'are extremely difficult to keep alive in captivity', and ' many of the animals rescued from traffickers die in zoos and rescue centres'.
Answer: B Paragraph B describes what 'many people assume' (rumination is a way of dealing with problems) and says ' Neither view is supported by the evidence '.
Answer: F Paragraph F: 'think about the problem from a distance, as if we were giving advice to a friend in the same situation '.
Answer: B Paragraph B: ' Brain-scanning research has also found that in people who ruminate heavily, a network of regions ... is unusually busy'.
Answer: thoughtful Paragraph B: 'Others regard it as a sign of a thoughtful personality.' 'An indication of' paraphrases 'a sign of'.
Answer: solutions Paragraph B: people who ruminate 'come up with fewer solutions , and they have less confidence in the ones they do produce'.
Answer: emotion Paragraph B: the network 'has stronger connections with areas involved in processing emotion '.
Answer: expectations Paragraph C: rumination is common among 'those who feel they must always meet other people's expectations '.
Answer: unresolved Paragraph C: 'Situations that remain unresolved ... are particularly likely to trigger it.' 'Still unresolved' paraphrases 'remain unresolved'.
Answer: productive Paragraph C: 'Part of the reason the habit persists is that it feels productive '. In reality, the negative feelings 'become stronger'.

text.en: It slows down the completion of everyday tasks.
It makes people more competitive with colleagues.
It causes people to delay making decisions.
It reduces people's interest in their careers.
It leads to disagreements with managers.

questions.explanation: Answer: A, C Paragraph D: office workers who ruminated ' took longer to complete routine tasks ' (A), and people who dwell on past mistakes ' tend to put off making choices ' (C). Competition, career interest and disagreements with managers are not mentioned.

text.en: not being critical of ourselves
writing our worries down in detail
discussing the problem repeatedly with friends
avoiding situations that cause stress
doing something brief that holds our attention

questions.explanation: Answer: A, E Paragraph F: ' a short, absorbing activity ... can interrupt the cycle' (E), and ' we should not criticise ourselves for ruminating' (A). Talking about the same worry again and again actually wears friends out (paragraph D), so C is wrong.
Answer: YES Paragraph 2: the governing body ' wanted to give its judges extra support rather than to replace them '.
Answer: NO Paragraph 2: 'Kovacs was still expected to watch each routine and enter her own marks '. The computer only provided 'a second opinion'.

Answer: NOT GIVEN Paragraph 3 lists landings as one of several things judges consider, and says they 'deduct points for each individual fault they see', but it never says which type of fault causes most deductions.

Answer: NO Paragraph 4: the sport is 'so controversial', and ' for decades , results at major championships have been followed by complaints about unfair scoring'. Disputes have been common, not unusual.

Answer: NOT GIVEN Paragraph 5 says 'younger audiences in particular are drifting towards other forms of entertainment', but it says nothing about whether they prefer television to watching competitions live.
Answer: YES Paragraph 9: 'it can be updated as the sport develops. If the rules change ... the software can simply be adjusted .'
Answer: F (digital model) Paragraph 1: beside Kovacs' score sheet was 'a screen showing a three-dimensional digital model of the gymnast'.
Answer: G (second opinion) Paragraph 2: 'The computer's role was to provide a second opinion '.
Answer: H (individual faults) Paragraph 3: for the execution score, 'judges deduct points for each individual fault they see'.
Answer: D (personal judgement) Paragraph 3: deciding how bent a leg was 'has always been a matter of personal judgement '. 'Fixed rules' (A) is the opposite idea.

Answer: B (frequent complaints) Paragraph 4: 'For decades, results at major championships have been followed by complaints about unfair scoring '. 'For decades' shows that they were frequent. Nationality is mentioned, but not national teams (C).

text.en: was originally collected for research purposes.
has helped judges to agree with each other more often.
is too complex for most viewers to understand.
could help the sport to attract a younger audience.

questions.explanation: Answer: D Paragraph 5: 'younger audiences in particular are drifting towards other forms of entertainment. The data produced by the sensors, she believes, could help to change this. ' She says the data makes performances easier to understand, the opposite of C.

text.en: It frequently makes mistakes when measuring small movements.
It may discourage gymnasts from attempting daring moves.
It will eventually lead to human judges being replaced.
It gives an advantage to gymnasts from certain countries.

questions.explanation: Answer: B Paragraph 7: the system is 'unforgiving', and Hale says that brave attempts used to receive credit, but ' Now it's all or nothing '. The implication is that gymnasts may be less willing to try daring moves. A is wrong because the system records tiny deviations accurately ('without fail').

text.en: to show that athletes and academics rarely share the same opinions
to argue that the system should be withdrawn from competitions
to suggest that precise scoring may not make a sport more enjoyable
to explain why gymnastics is losing its audience

questions.explanation: Answer: C Reyes says measuring performances 'changed what the sport is', and Park asks 'without risk, what is there to watch?'. The writer concludes: ' Accuracy clearly matters, but it may not be the only thing that makes a sport worth watching. ' The writer does not call for the system to be withdrawn (B).
